column4: The section's gaze cast to the ground is staged exactly as خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ: people emerge from the graves with eyes humbled, so free sight now is set against the resurrection procession.
أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ gives the same Last-Day state as the section: eyes themselves are humbled and unable to range freely.
The wrongdoers are brought before the Fire خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ and look مِن طَرْفٍ خَفِيٍّ; it supplies the section's precise union of humiliation and a furtive, constricted glance.
خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ repeats the image of lowered eyes under disgrace on the promised Day and shows that the bodily gaze reveals inward humiliation.
After the rush from the graves, خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ names the same downward gaze and disgrace that the section opposes to today's freedom to look.

The viewer sees the earth خَاشِعَةً, then sees it stir and grow when water descends; the root moves from a humbled gaze to low, lifeless ground and makes visible resurrection through the earth itself.
تَرَاهُمْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ وَهُمْ لَا يُبْصِرُونَ is the section's explicit empty form of looking: eyes are directed at the messenger while perception never occurs.
Some يَنظُرُ إِلَيْكَ yet remain blind and unseeing; this repeated scene confirms the section's distinction between turning the eye and gaining insight.
أَفَلَمْ يَنظُرُوا asks the same creation question as 88:17, directing sight upward to how the sky above was built, adorned, and left without fissures.

The question sends reflective sight into the dominion of the heavens and earth, then asks which report they will believe; it directly joins the world's visible order to the section's opening خبر/حديث.
The command to travel the earth and فَانظُرُوا كَيْفَ بَدَأَ الْخَلْقَ turns present observation of creation into evidence for the final creation, exactly the bridge developed in the section.
فَانظُرْ إِلَى آثَارِ رَحْمَتِ اللَّهِ asks the eye to watch dead earth revive and explicitly concludes that its reviver raises the dead.
عَلَى الْأَرَائِكِ يَنظُرُونَ places the Garden's people on couches looking freely, the section's afterlife destination for an eye no longer cast down.
The repeated عَلَى الْأَرَائِكِ يَنظُرُونَ makes the believers' Garden gaze part of the reversal of earthly mockery narrated in the surrounding passage.
إِلَى رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ gives the section's furthest possible destination of sight: radiant faces looking toward their Lord.
The viewer is commanded to return the gaze through the layered sky and ask whether any flaw can be seen, an exact enactment of thoughtful upward looking.
ثُمَّ ارْجِعِ الْبَصَرَ كَرَّتَيْنِ makes the eye range repeatedly before it returns خَاسِئًا وَهُوَ حَسِيرٌ; even free scrutiny ends humbled by the creation's integrity.
قُلِ انظُرُوا مَاذَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ sends the same present gaze through both upper and lower fields named in 88:18-20.
فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ mirrors the camel question by commanding a creature to look thoughtfully at how another familiar creature—himself—was made.
فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ إِلَى طَعَامِهِ redirects the same examining gaze to an everyday provision whose making the next verses unfold.
انظُرُوا إِلَى ثَمَرِهِ invites close sight of fruit forming and ripening after rain, making ordinary visible growth an intelligible sign rather than an empty spectacle.
أَلَمْ يَرَوْا إِلَى الطَّيْرِ holds an animal in the open sky before the eye, a close counterpart to looking at the camel below and the raised sky above.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا إِلَى الطَّيْرِ فَوْقَهُمْ directs sight explicitly overhead to wings spread and folded, joining animal form, upper direction, and sustaining creation.

Travel over the earth should produce hearts that understand and ears that hear; فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَعْمَى الْأَبْصَارُ locates failed vision in blind hearts, precisely explaining how one can look without seeing.
لَهُمْ أَعْيُنٌ لَا يُبْصِرُونَ بِهَا states the section's empty gaze in terms of unused eyes and places that failure among the marks of heedless creatures.
The guilty lower their heads before their Lord and say that they now see and hear; their too-late perception embodies the section's warning that today's mobile gaze will not remain available.
يَعْلَمُ خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ names the furtive treachery of eyes; it sharpens the hidden side-glance in 42:45 by adding that no covert movement of sight escapes God.

A mountain imagined receiving the Quran becomes خَاشِعًا مُتَصَدِّعًا; the section's gaze toward the erected mountain thus meets the same root that describes the lowered face and learns what true reception would do.
The question whether it is time for believing hearts to تَخْشَعَ voluntarily brings the section's future compelled humbling into the present interval when response is still possible.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ supplies the radiant faces whose action 75:23 completes by looking toward their Lord, reversing the humbled faces of 88:2.
The immediately opposed faces are بَاسِرَةٌ; beside the radiant gaze of 75:22-23, this ayah preserves the same two-face division that structures surah 88.
The warning fixes accountability on a day تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ الْأَبْصَارُ, another bodily fate of eyes when the present chance to observe and answer has ended.
The feared Day تَتَقَلَّبُ فِيهِ الْقُلُوبُ وَالْأَبْصَارُ makes both heart and eyesight overturn, joining the section's physical and inward senses of vision.
فَإِذَا بَرِقَ الْبَصَرُ portrays sight dazzled at the Hour, another precise loss of the calm, ranging gaze invited in the present.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُ عَيْنَيْنِ makes the two eyes themselves an object of the same creation question, so the instrument invited to inspect the camel must also be recognized as created.
ثُمَّ لَتَرَوُنَّهَا عَيْنَ الْيَقِينِ moves from present heedlessness to unavoidable eye-certainty at the Fire, showing the terrible endpoint of sight that refused reflection.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا كَيْفَ يُبْدِئُ اللَّهُ الْخَلْقَ asks people to perceive creation and repetition; 29:20 then tells them to walk the earth and inspect that beginning.
Continuing the upward look of 50:6, this ayah turns sight to the spread earth, set mountains, and growing pairs, closely matching 88:19-20.
تَبْصِرَةً وَذِكْرَى names the purpose of the sky-and-earth scene in 50:6-7: it is meant to produce sight and remembrance in a receptive servant.
After the visible rain and growth in 50:9-10, كَذَلِكَ الْخُرُوجُ explicitly identifies dead-land revival with emergence from the graves, joining creation-gaze to 54:7's procession.
The winds raise clouds, God spreads and fragments them, and rain comes through; this is the visible mercy whose آثار 30:50 tells the reader to inspect.
Creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for understanding minds, supplying the field over which the section asks sight to move.
Those minds remember God while contemplating the creation of heavens and earth; it states the thoughtful seeing that 3:190's signs and the section's questions seek.
God will show signs فِي الْآفَاقِ وَفِي أَنفُسِهِمْ until truth becomes clear, expanding the section's four-direction gaze into horizon and self.
وَفِي الْأَرْضِ آيَاتٌ لِّلْمُوقِنِينَ makes the earth below a readable field of signs, the point of the section's downward but unconfined look.
وَفِي أَنفُسِكُمْ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ adds the viewer to the earth-signs of 51:20 and asks directly why inwardly meaningful sight does not occur.
Its catalogue joins created heavens and earth, rain-revived ground, dispersed creatures, winds, and governed clouds as signs for reason—the same move from visible world to understanding.
The heavens and earth are signs for believers, directly matching the upper and lower objects to which the section releases the eye.
Human creation and the creatures God disperses are signs, adding the viewer and the camel-like animal world to the heavens and earth of 45:3.
Night, day, descending provision, revived earth, and changing winds complete 45:3-4's visible sequence as signs for people who understand.
God raised the heavens without visible pillars and subjected sun and moon; the ayah turns the section's upward question into a claim about what the observer can see.
God spread the earth, placed mountains and rivers, and made paired fruits; it closely restages the section's frontward and downward objects after 13:2's sky.
Adjacent plots and varied gardens watered by one water are declared signs for reason, demanding discriminating sight rather than mere surface looking.
The ayah gathers heavens raised without visible supports, mountains cast into earth, dispersed animals, rain, and plants—nearly the whole landscape traversed by 88:17-20.
أَأَنتُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمِ السَّمَاءُ answers resurrection doubt by asking whether humans or the constructed sky are harder to create, paralleling 88's كَيْفَ خُلِقَتْ.
God raised and proportioned the sky's structure, a close verbal and visual counterpart to 88:18 within the creation proof begun in 79:27.
وَالْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ دَحَاهَا turns the same proof downward to the spread earth, corresponding to 88:20.
وَالْجِبَالَ أَرْسَاهَا places fixed mountains between sky and earth in the sequence, corresponding to the frontward object of 88:19.
The oath by the sky and the One who built it condenses the same created upper object that 88:18 asks the viewer to inspect.
The next oath turns to the earth and the One who spread it, preserving the sky-to-ground movement of the section.
The heavens and earth are presented as once joined and then parted, and all life made from water; أَفَلَا يُؤْمِنُونَ demands belief from visible creation.
Firm mountains and broad paths are placed in earth so people may be guided, continuing 21:30's created landscape and matching 88's mountain and spread ground.
The sky is a protected roof, yet وَهُمْ عَنْ آيَاتِهَا مُعْرِضُونَ; the object stands open above while viewers turn away, the failure targeted by the section's question.
أَمْ خُلِقُوا مِنْ غَيْرِ شَيْءٍ asks the human creature the creation question from the other side: whether they arose from nothing or created themselves.
أَمْ خَلَقُوا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ follows 52:35 by setting the viewer against the same heavens and earth and exposing disbelief as failed certainty.
أَوَلَمْ يَتَفَكَّرُوا فِي أَنفُسِهِم asks for inward reflection on heavens, earth, truth, and a fixed term, articulating the thought that must accompany the section's looking.
أَلَمْ تَرَ traces rain into springs through earth, varied crops, withering, and debris; the whole visible cycle becomes a reminder for understanding minds.
أَلَمْ تَرَ begins with rain and opens into colored fruits and differently colored mountain tracts, making careful vision range from sky to the section's frontward mountains.
People, creatures, and cattle likewise differ in color, and true knowledge yields fear; it adds the camel's animal class to 35:27's observed world and names the inward result.
أَلَمْ تَرَ asks the viewer to recognize every being's glorification, with birds spreading wings in the sky; perception must reach the act expressed by the visible form.
أَلَمْ تَرَ follows clouds as they are driven, joined, heaped, and release rain and hail from above, training the mobile gaze in a staged natural process.
God turns night and day, and إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِّأُولِي الْأَبْصَارِ states that eyes should cross from alternation to lesson.
God creates every creature from water and varies its movement on belly, two legs, or four; this is a direct analogue to considering how the camel's form was created.
Heavens, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, creatures, and many people prostrate; the landscape of the section already bends willingly, while punishment falls on many who do not.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا asks people to watch created things cast shadows right and left in prostration while humbled, joining free directional sight to visible submission.
Every creature in heavens and earth, including the animals, prostrates without arrogance; it completes the shadow-prostration seen in 16:48.
God places constellations in the sky and adorns it لِلنَّاظِرِينَ, explicitly identifying the raised heaven as something made for observers.
For doubt about resurrection, the ayah directs attention to human formation and to barren earth that stirs and grows after rain, joining created body and reviving ground.
Because of the visible creation and earth-revival in 22:5, this ayah concludes that God is truth and gives life to the dead.
The proof of 22:5-6 culminates in the Hour and God's raising those in graves, linking today's observed ground to the humbled eyes emerging from it.
Winds raise clouds and drive them to dead land, which God revives; كَذَلِكَ النُّشُورُ explicitly reads the scene as resurrection.
The dead earth revived and producing grain is called a sign, making what people eat a visible witness to life after death.
After declaring that God revives earth after its death, the ayah says the signs have been made clear لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ, naming the understanding sought by the visual questions.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا asks whether the Creator of heavens and earth can create their like and gives them a fixed term, turning the cosmic gaze directly toward resurrection.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا asks whether the unwearied Creator of heavens and earth can revive the dead, an explicit inference from looking at creation.
أَوَلَيْسَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ بِقَادِرٍ asks the same creation-to-recreation question without naming the visual act.
The creation of heavens and earth is greater than human creation; this comparison explains why the section's upward and downward gaze answers doubt about return.
فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ closely doubles 88:12's flowing Garden spring and makes the عين/eye word audible in another paradisal scene.
فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ supplies the paired Garden's two gushing springs, preserving the section's spring/eye word while varying how water moves.
عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ is a Garden spring whose water God's servants cause to flow abundantly, a direct counterpart to 88:12.
عَيْنًا فِيهَا تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا identifies another named Garden spring, extending the section's attention to عين as both spring and eye.
عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا الْمُقَرَّبُونَ makes Tasnim a spring for those brought near, adjoining the same surah's couch-bound gaze in 83:23 and 83:35.
The question asks who can bring مَاءٍ مَّعِينٍ if water sinks away; the section's dictionary sense of maʿīn as water open to the eyes is placed against its disappearance underground.
No soul knows what قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ is hidden as reward; the eye that can inspect present signs cannot yet see the Garden joy prepared for it.
In the Garden are what souls desire and تَلَذُّ الْأَعْيُنُ; this gives the liberated afterlife eye not only range but enduring delight.
بَصَائِرُ have come from the Lord, so whoever sees benefits himself and whoever is blind bears it; this states the moral stake of perceptive versus empty looking.
When reminded of their Lord's signs, the faithful do not fall upon them deaf and blind; their receptive response is the opposite of eyes directed without insight.
The question imagines God taking hearing and sight and sealing hearts, then asks who could restore them; present visual freedom is thus a revocable gift.
God brings people out knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts so they may be grateful; the eye examining creation is itself a created means of response.
The Creator gives hearing, sight, and hearts, yet people give little thanks; the ayah places visual capacity inside the same creation argument as 67:3-4.
Heads are raised while the gaze does not return to them; this locked upward stare is the directional opposite of the section's ground-cast eye, yet both show sight stripped of freedom on that Day.
At the suddenly near true promise, the disbelievers' eyes are fixed in a stare; the section's lowered eye and this transfixed eye mark different forms of compelled Last-Day vision.
The covering is removed and فَبَصَرُكَ الْيَوْمَ حَدِيدٌ; Day-of-Judgment sight becomes piercing only after the present invitation to see has been refused.
أَسْمِعْ بِهِمْ وَأَبْصِرْ يَوْمَ يَأْتُونَنَا contrasts how sharply they will hear and see upon arrival with their manifest error today.
The guilty are مَحْجُوبُونَ from their Lord that Day, a precise boundary opposite the radiant faces looking toward their Lord in 75:23.
لَّا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ sets a boundary on visual comprehension while God comprehends all vision; it prevents the final gaze of 75:23 from being mistaken for optical mastery.
Moses asks أَنظُرْ إِلَيْكَ, is told he will not see, and is directed to the mountain that crumbles; present sight's limit, the mountain, and the promised ultimate gaze meet in one scene.
People pass by many signs in heavens and earth while turning away; the whole visual field is available, but their stance empties the gaze of attention.
Whoever turns from remembrance is raised blind, making the section's warning concrete: refusing sight while it is free ends in a Day when it cannot function.
The raised person asks why he is blind although he once could see; the question explicitly compares the lost present faculty with the state announced in 20:124.
God answers that the person forgot His signs and is therefore forgotten that Day, explaining the blindness of 20:124-125 as failed attention rather than lack of exposed signs.
Whoever is blind in this life is blind and further astray in the next; physical language becomes the boundary between present insight and final loss of way.
Their eyes were under a covering from God's remembrance and they could not hear, an inwardly blocked present gaze set against the section's open survey of signs.
Even if a gate in heaven opened and they continued ascending through it, the upward scene would exceed the section's invitation to look at the sky yet still fail to convince.
They would claim their eyes had been dazzled and they were bewitched; it completes 15:14 as an extreme case of seeing without perceptive assent.
Even seeing a fragment of sky falling, they call it a piled cloud; the sky is visibly before them, but interpretation protects denial from sight.
Believing men are commanded يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ; voluntary ethical lowering now distinguishes disciplined vision from the humiliating lowered eyes of the Last Day.
Believing women receive the same command to lower their sight, confirming that a constrained gaze can be chosen purity rather than imposed disgrace.
لَا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ forbids extending the eyes toward transient worldly enjoyments; the section's free gaze is therefore free for signs, not covetous wandering.
وَلَا تَعْدُ عَيْنَاكَ عَنْهُمْ forbids the Prophet's eyes from passing beyond those who call on God toward worldly adornment, setting an ethical limit within visual freedom.
The command not to extend both eyes toward the flower of worldly life bounds the present gaze by purpose and contrasts passing spectacle with the Lord's lasting provision.
The earth is burst into عُيُونًا in the Flood; the same spring word that marks Garden water becomes overwhelming judgment water, exposing the image's opposite potential.
كَمْ تَرَكُوا مِن جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ records gardens and springs abandoned by Pharaoh's people, a worldly version of the paradisal scene that cannot be kept.
Pharaoh's people are removed from جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ; the familiar garden-and-spring pair becomes a lost possession rather than the secure afterlife spring of the section.
Receptive hearers fall on their chins weeping and the revelation increases them خُشُوعًا; voluntary descent before the Quran now answers the involuntary lowered gaze later.
The believers are خَاشِعُونَ in prayer by choice, giving the root a present form of inward attentiveness opposite eschatological humiliation.
Hearing, eyes, and hearts availed the destroyed people nothing because they rejected God's signs; possessing the organs does not secure the reflective sight the section demands.
On the Day of summons, خَشَعَتِ الْأَصْوَاتُ and only a whisper is heard; the root that lowers the section's eyes also subdues the whole auditory scene.
Those given prior knowledge fall on their chins in prostration when the Quran is recited; 17:109 completes this bodily descent by naming increased خشوع.
Those with diseased hearts look at the Prophet نَظَرَ الْمَغْشِيِّ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ; fear turns directed sight into the constrained stare of someone overtaken by death.
In fear, eyes rotate like those of one fainting from death; the bodily distortion offers a worldly foretaste of the eye losing its free movement.
They are called to prostrate but cannot on the Day the ساق is uncovered; 68:43 then shows their eyes lowered under disgrace, so inability precedes the humbled gaze.
People rush from the graves as though racing to a marker; 70:44 supplies their lowered eyes, while this ayah contributes the direction and speed of the compelled movement.
Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and grain; it begins the visible revival that 50:11 identifies with emergence from graves.
Tall date palms with layered clusters continue the inspectable growth of 50:9 before 50:11 draws the resurrection conclusion.
People had been in despair immediately before the rain; the change supplies the human before-and-after against which 30:50 calls the new life آثار الرحمة.
Darkened night and brought-forth daylight make the raised sky of 79:27-28 visibly ordered before the passage turns to earth.
Water and pasture are brought from the spread earth of 79:30, showing what the downward gaze can discern in that prepared surface.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ closes the sky-earth-mountain sequence as provision for people and cattle, relating the viewed world to the camel's lived setting.
Night, day, sun, and moon each swim in an orbit, extending the protected sky of 21:32 from fixed roof to ordered motion.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا begins the process that 80:24 commands the human to inspect in his food.
ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْأَرْضَ شَقًّا turns the inspecting eye downward to the earth opened for growth.
Grain is grown from the split ground, the first visible answer to the food-question in 80:24.
Grapes and fresh herbage diversify the products the commanded gaze is meant to trace back to their making.
Olives and palms continue the visible catalogue of provision produced through water and opened earth.
Dense gardens enlarge the viewed scene beyond a single item of food.
Fruit and pasture join human food to the familiar animal environment evoked by the camel.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ names the whole observed sequence as provision for people and their cattle.
خُلِقَ مِن مَّاءٍ دَافِقٍ answers 86:5's command to inspect what the human was created from with an origin hidden inside the familiar body.
The fluid emerging from between backbone and ribs continues the precise bodily origin that reflective sight in 86:5 is to consider.
إِنَّهُ عَلَى رَجْعِهِ لَقَادِرٌ draws resurrection from the inspected first creation of 86:5-7, the same inference the section draws from created forms.
نَحْنُ خَلَقْنَاكُمْ فَلَوْلَا تُصَدِّقُونَ opens a sequence of direct creation questions by making the addressee's own createdness evidence for truth.
أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا تُمْنُونَ directs consideration to the seed of human life, beginning the concrete answer to 56:57.
The question asks whether people create that life or God does, paralleling the section's attention to how a creature is made.
Knowledge of the first creation should produce remembrance, explicitly turning origin into evidence after the intervening death-and-replacement claim.
أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا تَحْرُثُونَ redirects examining sight to the cultivated earth underfoot.
The question whether humans make the crop grow or God does uncovers agency behind the field viewed in 56:63.
أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ الْمَاءَ الَّذِي تَشْرَبُونَ makes everyday water another object of deliberate consideration, resonating with the section's visible flowing spring.
The question asks whether people bring water down from clouds or God does, connecting the drink in 56:68 to the sky above.
أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ continues the same disciplined seeing with the familiar fire people kindle.
The question whether people created its tree or God did again moves from a handled object to its created source.
God made that fire a reminder and provision, stating the cognitive and practical purposes of the object inspected in 56:71-72.
God splits grain and seed, brings living from dead and dead from living; the claim supplies the hidden creative action behind the fruit 6:99 tells people to watch.
Dawn, night, sun, and moon are precisely measured, moving the same sign-sequence through the sky before it reaches earthly growth.
Stars are made for guidance in the darkness of land and sea, assigning the upward gaze a practical as well as reflective direction.
Humanity's creation from one soul inserts the observer's own origin into the visible signs that culminate in 6:99.
The command to travel the earth and فَانظُرُوا see the deniers' outcome gives the section's free downward gaze a historical object: traces of moral consequence.
قُلْ سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ انظُرُوا sends the addressee over the earth to inspect the deniers' end, turning ground into testimony.
Travel and فَانظُرُوا at the deniers' outcome follows the history of messengers, so thoughtful sight reads destroyed communities as well as created forms.
The command to walk the earth and inspect the criminals' outcome uses the same active, mobile gaze but directs it toward moral history.
Travel and inspection reveal the outcome of earlier polytheists; the earth below retains evidence for a gaze willing to move through it.
The question asks whether they have traveled the earth and looked at former peoples' outcome, setting historical seeing beside the final abode promised to the mindful.
أَوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَيَنظُرُوا contrasts the greater works and cultivation of earlier peoples with the ruins their wrongdoing produced.
Traveling earth and looking at the stronger predecessors' outcome leads to God's unfrustrated power in heavens and earth.
